newsitem.title: UK: Major faces last poll test before UK election.
newsitem.headline: Major faces last poll test before UK election.

text.p: The ruling Conservative party was braced on Thursday for defeat in a by-election that is the last test of public opinion before Britain's general election.

Prime Minister John Major is expected to hold the election on May 1 and Thursday's ballot in Wirral South in northwest England will be an important guide to whether his party stands any chance of winning an unprecedented fifth term in office.
As voters cast their ballots, opinion polls suggested Labour would capture what has hitherto been a safe Conservative seat.

Opposition Labour leader Tony Blair called on voters in Wirral South -- a prosperous corner of middle England across the River Mersey from Liverpool -- to send a message that it was time for a change after 18 years of unbroken Conservative rule.

"They can deliver a crushing verdict on this weak, divided and discredited Tory party -- and take a huge step towards giving our country a new government and a new future," Blair wrote in the Daily Mirror newspaper.
Ministers have been playing down expectations for the Wirral South vote, pointing out that voters at by-elections regularly punish the government of the day.
Conservative strategists hope to be able to portray a narrow defeat as a turning point in the party's fortunes. But with the general election clock ticking, Major has a mountain to climb.
A MORI opinion poll in Thursday's Times newspaper showed national support for the Conservatives at 31 percent, 21 points behind Labour.
Although Labour's lead narrowed by four percentage points from January, Major could draw little comfort since it was still within the recent range of fluctuations, The Times said.
"Moreover, no party has ever reversed such a big gap in the closing weeks before a general election," the paper's political commentator, Peter Riddell, wrote.
The loss of Wirral South would put Major into a minority in the lower House of Commons. The Conservatives would have 322 votes, one fewer than all the opposition parties combined.
But Major would probably still be able to solider on and call the general election on a date of his choosing.
To oust Major and force an early election, Labour would have to persuade all the smaller opposition parties to side with it in a vote of confidence.
The Ulster Unionists, the biggest party representing Northern Ireland's pro-British Protestant majority, would hold the key because they usually support the Conservatives.
On Thursday Ulster Unionist leader David Trimble was careful not to fan speculation that he might hasten the government's demise.
He said Blair had not discussed with him what attitude the Ulster Unionists would take to a possible a no-confidence motion if Labour does indeed capture Wirral South.

"I am sure Labour will want to stage some sort of demonstration after the (Wirral) result, but I don't get the feeling that Labour will be going all out to bring the government down early," he told reporters.

Asked whether he personally was closer to the Conservatives than to Labour, Trimble said the policy differences between the two parties were now very narrow. "We have to work with whoever is in power," he said.
